sections.h2: Who bills property tax in Jacksonville?
sections.html:
The Duval County Tax Collector bills and collects Jacksonville property tax, while the Duval County Property Appraiser sets the value and decides exemptions. The tax collector's own page says taxing authorities such as the City of Jacksonville and the school board set the rate from their budgets.

Three offices matter when you sell a Jacksonville house with a tax question open:

  • The tax collector, at 231 E. Forsyth Street, Jacksonville, FL 32202, answers bill and payoff questions at (904) 255-5700, option 4. The main office is open Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
  • The property appraiser's exemptions desk, reached at (904) 255-5900, handles homestead status and mailing-address changes.
  • The Value Adjustment Board clerk, at 117 West Duval Street, Suite 305, takes value and exemption appeals.

The tax collector also runs branch offices around the city, including a newer St. Johns Square branch at 11160 Beach Blvd., Suite 121, that replaced two older locations in 2026. Check the branch list before you drive across town to pay a bill in person.

sections.h2: When are Jacksonville property taxes due, and what discounts apply?
sections.html:
Jacksonville property tax is assessed on the January 1 value, billed in November, and payable without penalty through March 31 of the following year. Paying early earns a discount that shrinks each month.

Early payment schedule printed by the Duval County Tax Collector (taxcollector.jacksonville.gov, Real Estate Taxes page)
Payment monthDiscount
November4%
December3%
January2%
February1%
MarchNone (gross amount)

Because the bill covers a calendar year, a Jacksonville seller who closes in spring or summer is usually settling a bill that has already been issued the prior November. Ask the title company whether that bill was paid, and at which discount tier, before you accept a closing statement.

sections.h2: What happens if Jacksonville property tax goes unpaid?
sections.html:
Unpaid current taxes turn delinquent on April 1, and the collector adds a minimum mandatory 3% interest fee on top of advertising costs. Anything still unpaid goes into the annual tax certificate sale, held on or before June 1.

The 2026 Duval sale was scheduled for May 27, 2026, with online registration through a bidding site the collector names on its page. Bidders in that sale compete on the lowest interest rate they will accept, so the winner holds a lien rather than the house itself. A certificate has to sit for two years from April 1 of the issue year before its holder can apply for a tax deed. Duval's tax deed sales are run by the Duval County Clerk of Court.

Two details matter to an owner in trouble:

  • The collector's page states that homestead liens are not subject to the sale of tax certificates.
  • A certificate holder may not contact the owner about the debt until two years after April 1 of the issue year, so a stranger demanding payment earlier is breaking the rule.

Florida law also lets the bidder's interest accrue after the sale, and an owner who redeems pays the certificate amount plus interest. Ask the tax collector for a current payoff figure instead of estimating one.

sections.h2: Can I pay Jacksonville property tax in installments?
sections.html:
Yes. If your estimated tax is over $100, you can prepay in four installments, but you must apply on or before April 30 of the year you elect to prepay. Apply online through your account search, by email to taxdept@coj.net, or by mail to Installment Processing at the tax collector's Forsyth Street address.

Installment schedule printed by the Duval County Tax Collector (Installment Payments page)
InstallmentDue dateDiscount
FirstJune 306%
SecondSeptember 304.5%
ThirdDecember 313%
FourthMarch 310%

The page adds a July 31 date with no discount: if the first installment is not paid by then, the account drops out of the plan without penalty and is billed annually in November. Once you pay the first installment you must stay on the plan for the full year, and a missed payment rolls into the next one with no discount. Accounts already on the plan renew automatically.

For a partial payment outside the plan, the Value Adjustment Board's page tells owners to contact the tax collector first.

sections.h2: How do I challenge my Jacksonville property value?
sections.html:
You have 25 days from the mailing of the Notice of Proposed Property Taxes, the TRIM notice, to file a petition with the Value Adjustment Board. The deadline is printed at the bottom right of your notice, and the board does not treat a postmark as timely filing.

For 2026 that deadline was Tuesday, September 8, 2026, so it has passed. The window follows the same pattern each year: the notice goes out in August and the petition is due in early September. Late petitions need a written good-cause explanation and supporting documents.

  • The filing fee is up to $50 per parcel, and it is not refundable.
  • No fee applies to a homeowner who timely appeals a homestead exemption denial.
  • The property appraiser offers an informal review first and cannot accept the petition itself.
  • Foreclosures and distressed sales are not counted as qualified sales when the appraiser values neighboring homes, though the appraiser still values the property at market value.

The board has five members: two Jacksonville City Council members, one Duval County School Board member and two citizen appointees.

sections.h2: How do homestead and Save Our Homes work in Jacksonville?
sections.html:
A Jacksonville homeowner who lives in the house on January 1 and applies by March 1 can claim Florida's homestead exemption of up to $50,000. The first $25,000 reduces every tax, including school tax, and the second $25,000 applies only to value above $50,000 and only to non-school taxes.

The Save Our Homes cap limits yearly growth in assessed value on a homestead to the lower of 3 percent or inflation. The state revenue department's chart shows the 2026 cap at 2.7 percent. The Duval appraiser's FAQ explains the gap between market value and assessed value as the deferral that builds up for long-time owners, and notes that a change in ownership removes it.

That is the part that matters to a seller. A buyer starts at full market value the following January 1, so the buyer's first bill can be much higher than yours. The appraiser's FAQ lists other ways a cap can disappear, including a homestead exemption that is removed after a change of ownership and market value falling to meet assessed value.

Non-homestead property has its own 10 percent annual limit on assessed value, which also resets on a change of ownership. A rental house in Jacksonville therefore behaves differently from an owner-occupied one when it sells.

sections.h2: What happens to the tax when I sell a Jacksonville house?
sections.html:
The title company pays any unpaid tax from your sale proceeds and prorates the current year between you and the buyer. The tax bill itself goes to the owner of record, so the closing statement is where the seller's share of the year gets credited to the buyer.

Start with these steps:

  • Request a payoff from the tax collector, and ask whether back taxes or a lien certificate sit on the account.
  • If you are on the installment plan, tell the closing agent which installments are paid. Ask the tax collector how the plan is handled after a sale.
  • Confirm whether any non-ad valorem charges, such as stormwater or solid waste fees, appear on the bill.
  • Look up the parcel in the clerk's Official Records for liens or other recorded claims.

Florida's deed stamp tax is 70 cents on each $100 of consideration, and all parties to the document are liable, whichever side agrees to pay. Recording fees charged by the clerk are $5.00 for the first page and $4.00 for each additional page, plus per-page technology and modernization charges set in the statute.

A cash buyer who closes as-is can often work to a date that fits your tax calendar, which matters when a delinquency date or certificate sale is close.

sections.h2: What is the Jacksonville millage rate?
sections.html:
The tax collector does not publish the rate on its own page. Its millage charts page says the charts are maintained by the Property Appraiser and are on that office's website, so use that chart or your own bill for the figure.

A mill is $1 of tax per $1,000 of taxable value. Your Jacksonville bill adds the rates of every taxing authority covering your parcel, so a neighbor in a different district can pay a different total. Ask the property appraiser or the tax collector's office for your parcel's combined rate before you project a payoff.

faqs.q: When does Jacksonville property tax become delinquent?
faqs.a: On April 1 following the assessment year. The collector adds a minimum 3% interest fee plus advertising costs at that point, and unpaid accounts head to the tax certificate sale on or before June 1.

faqs.q: Is there a discount for paying early in Jacksonville?
faqs.a: Yes, 4% in November, 3% in December, 2% in January and 1% in February, with no discount in March. The tax collector's Real Estate Taxes page prints this schedule.

faqs.q: Can a Jacksonville homestead be sold to a tax certificate buyer?
faqs.a: No. The tax collector's page states that homestead liens are not subject to the sale of tax certificates. The unpaid tax still has to be settled, and a tax deed requires a certificate that has aged at least two years.

faqs.q: What should I do if the Jacksonville bill is wrong?
faqs.a: Call the property appraiser for an informal review first, then file with the Value Adjustment Board by the date on your TRIM notice. For a bill that is correct but unaffordable, ask the tax collector about the installment plan or a partial payment agreement.

faqs.q: Who pays Jacksonville property tax at closing?
faqs.a: The title company usually settles it on the closing statement, charging each side for its share of the year and paying any back tax from the seller's proceeds. Ask the closing agent for the payoff figure in writing.
